intro: Elgar titled the finale of his “Enigma” Variations “E.D.U.” after Edoo, the name his wife Alice used for him. Alice’s music and Jaeger’s, belonging to the two people who kept him composing, return within it.

sections.label: Var 14 · “E.D.U.”, Finale: Allegro
sections.mNote: Short violin and bassoon figures over a detached bass

sections.label: Link · Quiet winds and divided cellos
sections.mNote: Soft cello quavers continue beneath the wind phrases

sections.label: Var 14 · Animando, strings
sections.mNote: Woodwinds and horns join the string phrase as it grows.

sections.label: Coda · G major, full orchestra
sections.mNote: The bass holds G beneath the final chords.

cues.title: Opening of the finale
cues.text: Elgar’s own variation begins softly at rehearsal 61, Allegro. Short phrases pass between first violins, cellos and bassoons above detached notes in the bass. The trombones and tuba are marked ppp.
cues.evidence: Novello full score, p. 93, rehearsal 61: Allegro, soft string and bassoon figures, detached low strings and brass marked ppp.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Elgar’s nickname, “Edoo”
cues.text: E.D.U. is Elgar’s spelling of Edoo, Alice’s pet name for him. He placed himself last of the fourteen portraits. At the time he was teaching violin, and he described the variation as his answer to discouragement about his musical future.
cues.evidence: The nickname and subject: https://elgar.org/3enigma.htm. Elgar’s own commentary describes the variation as his answer to discouragement about his musical future: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enigma_Variations, variation XIV.

cues.title: Recollections of C.A.E. and Nimrod
cues.text: The finale, Elgar’s self-portrait, recalls two earlier variations: Alice’s, C.A.E., and Jaeger’s, Nimrod. Their broad melodies return among the quick figures of Edoo’s theme.
cues.evidence: Elgar identifies the recollections of variations I and IX in his commentary on the finale, reproduced at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enigma_Variations. This note concerns the finale as a whole.
cues.how: About the passage as a whole.

cues.title: Woodwind over divided cellos
cues.text: The full texture thins to woodwind phrases above divided cellos, which play soft quavers in the Allegro tempo. When the first violins return, Elgar marks them pianississimo, non legato, very soft with the notes kept separate.
cues.evidence: Novello full score, p. 111, approach to rehearsal 73: woodwind solos over divided cellos, followed by first violins marked ppp non legato.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Revised ending, Worcester, 1899
cues.text: After the London première, Jaeger persuaded Elgar to enlarge the ending. Elgar added ninety-six bars and an organ part, which is optional in the published score. He conducted the expanded version himself at the Worcester Three Choirs Festival on 13 September 1899.
cues.evidence: The revision, its extent and the Worcester performance are documented at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enigma_Variations, citing Michael Kennedy and the work’s performance history. The organ is optional in the published score.

cues.title: Final chords in G major
cues.text: The full orchestra plays chords of G major. The bass holds G while the upper parts finish their last phrases, and a timpani roll makes a crescendo beneath the final chord. Elgar lets the chord sound, then cuts it off.
cues.evidence: Novello full score, pp. 126–128: concluding G-major chords, a sustained tonic bass and the final timpani crescendo.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: Divided cellos and basses before rehearsal 73
transitions.to: Link · Quiet winds and divided cellos
transitions.how: The rushing string phrases give way to repeated soft quavers in the divided cellos and basses. Above them, oboes, clarinets and bassoons play phrases marked espressivo. The Allegro tempo continues. At rehearsal 73 the violins, very quiet, take over the melody over pizzicato bass notes.
transitions.evidence: Novello full score, p. 111, before and at rehearsal 73: repeated low-string quavers, expressive woodwind phrases and the violin return over pizzicato bass.

transitions.title: Animando at rehearsal 74
transitions.from: Link · Quiet winds and divided cellos
transitions.how: Low brass and timpani hold a soft chord while the violins’ short figures diminish. At animando (rehearsal 74) the cellos play a rising figure and the basses play arco again. Woodwinds and horns take up the rising phrase, and a new crescendo begins.
transitions.evidence: Novello full score, p. 113, rehearsal 74: sustained low brass before animando, arco basses, rising cello and wind figures, and crescendo.

transitions.title: Tonic pedal on G
transitions.how: The closing phrases are in G major. The brass sustain the chords while the strings play their last runs, and a held G stays in the bass. Elgar marks ritardando, then writes a final crescendo in the low winds and timpani before the orchestra’s last attack.
transitions.evidence: Novello full score, pp. 126–128, rehearsals 82–83 and the final bars: G-major conclusion, tonic pedal, ritardando and the final crescendo.

source.title: Elgar, Enigma Variations, full score (Novello)
source.locator: Novello full score, pp. 93–128, rehearsal figures 61–83: the expanded finale, including the quiet middle passage and G-major close.

timeline.note: Quiet phrases pass between first violins, cellos and bassoons above detached bass notes (p. 93).
Wind and brass join the rising string figures (pp. 94–96).
Horns, trumpets and violins play the broad tune, with percussion punctuating the phrases (pp. 96–99).
Strings and woodwinds take over while trumpets and trombones rest (pp. 100–102).
Wind and brass hold longer phrases above the running strings (pp. 103–108).
Fast violin runs meet accented chords from the full orchestra (pp. 109–110).
Cellos and basses repeat quiet quavers beneath expressive wind phrases (p. 111).
Quiet brass chords join the sustained wind melody and moving strings (pp. 112–113).
Marked animando, strings and winds climb together as the basses return to bowing (pp. 113–115).
Horns, trumpets and violins play above the full orchestra and percussion (pp. 116–119).
The strings race beneath broad wind and brass chords (pp. 120–125).
Brass chords sound over a held tonic bass and a timpani roll that grows louder in the G-major close (pp. 126–128).

composer.epithet: Composer of the Enigma Variations, a set of variations drawn from his friendships, who also recorded his own music for the gramophone.
facts: His father’s Worcester music shop; violin and organ; composition largely self-taught
Powick bandmaster, instrumental teacher and organist at St George’s, Worcester
Two symphonies; violin and cello concertos; Gerontius; five Pomp and Circumstance marches
Master of the King’s Musick from 1924; recordings of his own orchestral works
composer.background:
Elgar grew up among the instruments and sheet music in his father’s Worcester shop. William tuned pianos and played the organ at St George’s Catholic Church; Edward studied the scores, learned several instruments and earned money with his violin. Born at Lower Broadheath on 2 June 1857, he had hoped to study at Leipzig, but the family could not afford it. Playing in the Three Choirs Festival orchestra, he learned the choral music of Handel and Mendelssohn as a member of the string section.

From 1879 to 1884 he was bandmaster at Worcester County Asylum, Powick. He trained members of staff to play for the patients and supplied quadrilles and polkas for the Friday-evening dances. He knew each player in this orchestra individually and had to write within their capabilities. He also taught in local schools and gave private lessons in Malvern. In 1885 he succeeded William at the organ of St George’s.
